title: Congress
note: Sample section (Prompt 4, frame R32Path), extended in Prompt 12 with the rest of Unit 2's Congress questions. Every lesson is a draft until a person reviews it (content/course/README.md). Read it / Write it sentences use only the official USCIS word lists (content/vocab/).

listen.explanationKey: What part of the federal government writes laws?
facts: Congress is the legislative branch of the federal government.
Congress writes the laws for the whole country.
Congress can declare war and makes the federal budget.

newWords.meaning: the group of people who write the country's laws
the part of the government that makes laws
a plan for how to spend money
the building in Washington, D.C., where Congress meets

story.say: The federal government has three branches.

help.simpler: The national government is split into three parts.
help.example: The three parts are Congress, the President and the courts.
help.why: Knowing the three branches helps you answer many questions on the test.

story.say: Congress is the legislative branch.

help.simpler: “Legislative” means law-making. Congress is the part that makes laws.
help.example: When people talk about lawmakers in Washington, D.C., they mean Congress.
help.why: The test asks what part of the federal government writes laws. The answer is Congress.

story.say: Congress writes the laws for the whole country.

help.simpler: Congress makes the laws that everyone in the country must follow.
help.example: Congress writes a bill. If the President signs it, it becomes a law.
help.why: “Writes laws” is one answer when the test asks for a power of Congress.

check.statement: Congress writes the laws for the whole country.

story.say: Congress can declare war.

help.simpler: Only Congress can officially say the country is at war.
help.example: In 1941, Congress declared war after the attack on Pearl Harbor.
help.why: “Declares war” is another power of Congress on the test.

story.say: Congress also makes the federal budget: the plan for how to spend the government’s money.

help.simpler: Congress decides how the government spends its money.
help.example: The budget pays for things like the military, national parks and highways.
help.why: “Makes the federal budget” is another power of Congress on the test.

listen.explanationKey: What are the two parts of the U.S. Congress?
facts: Congress has two parts: the Senate and the House of Representatives.
The House of Representatives has 435 voting members.
Both parts meet in the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C.

newWords.meaning: one part of Congress, with 100 senators
the other part of Congress, with 435 voting members
a member who can vote on new laws

story.say: Congress has two parts.

help.simpler: Congress is made of two groups.
help.example: The two groups are the Senate and the House of Representatives.
help.why: The test asks you to name the two parts of Congress.

story.say: One part is the Senate.

help.simpler: The first part is called the Senate. Its members are senators.
help.example: Each state sends two senators to the Senate.
help.why: “The Senate” is one half of the answer about the two parts of Congress.

story.say: The other part is the House of Representatives.

help.simpler: The second part is the House of Representatives. Its members are representatives.
help.example: People often just call it “the House.”
help.why: “The House of Representatives” is the other half of the answer.

check.prompt: What are the two parts of Congress?
choices: The Senate and the House of Representatives

story.say: The House of Representatives has 435 voting members.

help.simpler: There are 435 voting members in the House.
help.example: States with more people have more of these members.
help.why: The test asks how many voting members the House has. The answer is 435.

story.say: Both parts meet in the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C.

help.simpler: Senators and representatives work in the same building, the U.S. Capitol.
help.example: The Capitol is the large white building with a dome in Washington, D.C.
help.why: Knowing where Congress meets helps you picture how it works.

check.statement: The House of Representatives has 100 voting members.

listen.explanationKey: How many U.S. senators are there?
facts: There are 100 U.S. senators.
Each state has two senators.
Big states and small states have the same number of senators.

newWords.meaning: a member of the Senate
one of the 50 parts of the United States

story.say: There are 100 U.S. senators.

help.simpler: The Senate has 100 members.
help.example: That is 50 states times 2 senators each.
help.why: The test asks how many senators there are. The answer is 100.

story.say: Each state has two senators.

help.simpler: Every state has exactly two senators.
help.example: California has two senators, and so does Wyoming.
help.why: This is why there are 100 senators in all.

check.prompt: How many senators does each state have?

story.say: Big states and small states have the same number of senators.

help.simpler: A state’s size does not change how many senators it has.
help.example: A state with millions of people and a state with far fewer people both have two.
help.why: This gives every state an equal voice in the Senate.

story.say: 50 states with two senators each make 100 senators.

help.simpler: Two senators for each of the 50 states makes 100.
help.example: If you remember 2 per state, you can find 100: 50 times 2.
help.why: It is an easy way to remember the answer on the test.

check.statement: A big state has more senators than a small state.

readIt.sentence: How many Senators does a state have?

listen.explanationKey: How long is a term for a U.S. senator?
facts: A U.S. senator's term is six years.
A member of the House of Representatives has a two-year term.
Voters can elect them again when the term ends.

newWords.meaning: the number of years a person serves in a job
to choose someone by voting

story.say: A senator’s term is six years.

help.simpler: A senator serves for six years at a time.
help.example: A senator elected in 2024 serves until early 2031.
help.why: The test asks how long a senator’s term is. The answer is six years.

story.say: A term is the number of years a person serves in a job.

help.simpler: A term is how long someone holds a job before the next election.
help.example: A senator’s term is six years. A President’s term is four years.
help.why: You need the word “term” to understand many test questions.

story.say: A member of the House of Representatives has a two-year term.

help.simpler: A member of the House serves for two years at a time.
help.example: There is an election for every House seat every two years.
help.why: The test asks about representatives too: their term is two years.

check.prompt: How long is a senator’s term?

story.say: When the term ends, voters can elect them again.

help.simpler: When a term ends, people vote again. The same person can win again.
help.example: A senator can be elected again and again, for many six-year terms.
help.why: Senators have no limit on how many terms they can serve.

check.statement: A member of the House of Representatives has a two-year term.

readIt.sentence: Who elects the Senators of a state?

writeIt.sentence: Citizens elect the Senators of the state.

listen.explanationKey: Who is one of your state’s U.S. senators now?
facts: Every state has two U.S. senators, and every congressional district has one representative.
These names change after elections, so Pathways looks them up from an official list.
Check the names again before your interview.

newWords.meaning: one area of a state that elects one representative
a member of the House of Representatives

story.say: Every state has two U.S. senators.

help.simpler: Each state has two senators in Washington, D.C.
help.example: Both senators from your state speak for everyone in your state.
help.why: The test may ask you to name one of your state’s senators.

story.say: Every congressional district has one representative.

help.simpler: Each area of a state, called a district, has one representative.
help.example: A big city may have several districts. A small state may have just one.
help.why: The test may also ask you to name your representative.

check.prompt: How many U.S. senators does your state have?

story.say: These names change after elections, so Pathways looks them up from an official list.

help.simpler: Senators can change after an election, so the app checks an official list.
help.example: If a senator retires, a new person takes the seat after the next election.
help.why: Always use today’s names when you answer the officer.

story.say: These are your state’s two senators today.

help.simpler: These two people are your state’s senators right now.
help.example: You can say either name when the officer asks for one of your senators.
help.why: The test asks you to name one of your state’s U.S. senators.

story.say: Check the names again before your interview.

help.simpler: Look at the names again just before your interview.
help.example: If there was an election, a name may be different.
help.why: You want to give the names of the senators serving on your interview day.

writeIt.sentence: We elect the Senators of our state.

listen.explanationKey: Who does a U.S. senator represent?
facts: A U.S. senator speaks for all the people of their state.
Citizens of the state vote to choose their senators.

newWords.meaning: to speak and act for a group of people
a person who is a member of a country

story.say: A U.S. senator speaks for all the people of their state.

help.simpler: A senator works for everyone who lives in the state.
help.example: A senator from Texas speaks for people all across Texas.
help.why: The test asks who a senator represents: all people of the state.

story.say: Not just one city or one district: everyone in the state.

help.simpler: Not just one town or area. The whole state.
help.example: People in big cities and small towns have the same two senators.
help.why: This is the difference between a senator and a representative.

story.say: Citizens of the state vote to choose their senators.

help.simpler: The people of the state choose their senators in an election.
help.example: Citizens vote for senators on Election Day in November.
help.why: This is one way the people control the government.

check.prompt: Who does a U.S. senator represent?
choices: All the people of their state

writeIt.sentence: The people of the state elect the Senators.

listen.explanationKey: Who does a member of the House of Representatives represent?
facts: Each state is cut into areas called congressional districts.
A member of the House of Representatives speaks for the people in one district.
Citizens in the district vote to choose their representative.

newWords.meaning: one area of a state that elects one representative
a member of the House of Representatives

story.say: Each state is cut into areas called congressional districts.

help.simpler: Each state is split into areas. Each area is a congressional district.
help.example: A state with many people has many districts. A small state may have just one.
help.why: Districts decide who your representative is.

story.say: A member of the House of Representatives speaks for the people in one district.

help.simpler: Your representative works for the people in your district.
help.example: Someone across town may be in a different district, with a different representative.
help.why: The test asks who a representative represents: the citizens in their district.

check.prompt: Who does a member of the House represent?

story.say: Citizens in the district vote to choose their representative.

help.simpler: People in the district choose their representative by voting.
help.example: There is an election for representatives every two years, in November.
help.why: This keeps representatives close to the people they serve.

check.statement: Each state is cut into areas called congressional districts.

listen.explanationKey: Some states have more representatives than other states. Why?
facts: States with more people have more representatives in the House.
Every state has two senators, big or small. This gives small states an equal voice.
This plan is called the Great Compromise.

newWords.meaning: how many people live in a place
the same for everyone
an agreement where each side gets part of what it wants

story.say: When the Constitution was written, big states and small states disagreed.

help.simpler: When the Constitution was written, big and small states did not agree.
help.example: They argued about how many votes each state should get in Congress.
help.why: This argument explains why Congress has two parts.

story.say: Big states wanted more seats for states with more people.

help.simpler: Big states wanted more votes because they had more people.
help.example: A state with many people wanted more seats than a state with few people.
help.why: This idea became the House of Representatives.

story.say: Small states wanted every state to have the same number.

help.simpler: Small states wanted every state to have the same number of votes.
help.example: A small state did not want bigger states to always outvote it.
help.why: This idea became the Senate.

choices: The same number for every state

story.say: The Great Compromise gave both: the House by population, and two senators for every state.

help.simpler: A compromise means each side gets part of what it wants.
help.example: The House counts people. The Senate gives every state two seats.
help.why: This compromise is why the House and the Senate have different numbers.

story.say: So states with more people have more representatives in the House.

help.simpler: States with more people get more members in the House.
help.example: California has many representatives. Wyoming has one.
help.why: This is why the 435 House seats are divided by population.

story.say: And every state has two senators, big or small. This gives small states an equal voice.

help.simpler: Every state has two senators, no matter its size.
help.example: Wyoming and California each have two senators.
help.why: The Senate gives small states an equal voice.

check.statement: Every state has the same number of senators.

readIt.sentence: What state has the most people?

listen.explanationKey: Why do U.S. representatives serve shorter terms than U.S. senators?
facts: Representatives serve two-year terms. Senators serve six-year terms.
Short terms mean representatives face voters often, so they follow what the public thinks.

newWords.meaning: what most people think about something
the number of years a person serves in a job

story.say: Representatives serve two-year terms.

help.simpler: Representatives serve for two years at a time.
help.example: A representative elected in November faces the next election two years later.
help.why: The test asks why representatives serve shorter terms.

story.say: Senators serve six-year terms.

help.simpler: Senators serve for six years at a time.
help.example: That is three times as long as a representative’s term.
help.why: Comparing the two helps you remember both numbers.

check.prompt: How long is a representative’s term?

story.say: Short terms mean representatives face voters often.

help.simpler: Representatives must ask voters for their votes every two years.
help.example: If voters are unhappy, they can choose someone new soon.
help.why: This is part of why representatives have short terms.

story.say: So they follow what the public thinks.

help.simpler: They pay close attention to what people want.
help.example: If many people in a district care about a new road, their representative listens.
help.why: The test asks why representatives serve shorter terms: to more closely follow public opinion.

check.statement: Representatives face voters every six years.

readIt.sentence: When do people vote for Congress?

listen.explanationKey: What is the name of the Speaker of the House of Representatives now?
facts: The Speaker leads the House of Representatives.
These names change after elections, so Pathways looks them up on an official list.
Check the names again before your interview.

newWords.meaning: the leader of the House of Representatives

story.say: The Speaker leads the House of Representatives.

help.simpler: The Speaker is the leader of the House of Representatives.
help.example: The Speaker runs the meetings of the House.
help.why: The test asks for the name of the Speaker of the House now.

story.say: These names change after elections.

help.simpler: The Speaker can change after an election.
help.example: The members of the House vote to choose their Speaker.
help.why: Always use today’s name when you answer.

story.say: So Pathways looks them up on an official list.

help.simpler: The app checks the name on an official list, so it is up to date.
help.example: The picture shows the name from that list.
help.why: You do not need to remember old names, only the current one.

story.say: Check the names again before your interview.

help.simpler: Look at the name again just before your interview.
help.example: If the House chose a new Speaker, the name will be different.
help.why: You want to give the name of the Speaker on your interview day.
